summary: This document explains how the experimental TCP option codepoints can serve several TCP extensions at once, even on one connection, using a new IANA TCP experiment identifier. It works with experiments that are not registered and those that do not use sharing. It is recommended for all new TCP options that use these codepoints.

eli5.summary: Several experiments share one mailbox, so each adds its own name tag to tell whose message is whose.

questions: shared use of experimental tcp options
what is a tcp experiment identifier
what is an exid in tcp
can multiple tcp experiments share options
subtitle: A tag field that lets many TCP experiments share the two experimental option codepoints.

tldr.problem: TCP has only two experimental option codepoints (253 and 254), and several experiments already collide on them, leaving each use ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: Each experimental option starts with a 16-bit or 32-bit experiment identifier (ExID), registered first come, first served with IANA, which receivers match to pick the right processing.
tldr.outcome: Experiments can coexist, even on one connection, and unmatched ExIDs are ignored. Public deployments MUST use ExIDs.

today: RFC 6994 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) from August 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the ExID mechanism for options built on the experimental codepoints from RFC 4727.

sections.title: The Problem with Two Experimental Codepoints
sections.content:
TCP options are identified by a one-byte value, so there are 256 possible codepoints and only 30 were assigned when this RFC was published. Two of them, 253 and 254, are set aside for experiments, testing, or cases where an assigned codepoint is not warranted or available.

There was no mechanism for sharing them. Options 253 and 254 were already deployed in operational code for an early version of TCP authentication, and 253 is also documented for the TCP Cookie Transaction option in RFC 6013. A single codepoint could then appear several times in one segment, each use ambiguous.

Some people also "squat" on unassigned codepoints, such as 31-32 and 76-78, and the RFC says this affects legitimate assignees. The RFC expects the misuse to continue, so its approach needs no extra codepoints and tolerates experiments that do not register or do not support it.
sections.eli5: Only two mailboxes were set aside for science projects, and many projects started stuffing letters into them. Nobody could tell whose letter was whose.

sections.title: The ExID Field
sections.content:
Normal TCP options start with a Kind byte and a Length byte. For the experimental codepoints (253 and 254), this RFC adds an experiment identifier right after them. The ExID is either 2 bytes (16 bits) or 4 bytes (32 bits), and the rest of the option content follows.

The rules in the RFC:

  • Protocols that need option codepoints but are not eligible for assigned ones SHOULD use 253 and 254 with ExIDs.
  • All protocols using them, even in controlled environments, SHOULD use ExIDs.
  • Protocols deployed outside controlled environments, such as the public Internet, MUST use ExIDs.
  • All ExIDs in use MUST be registered with IANA.

The ExID counts as part of the option, not the option header, so it increases the effective Length by its size and is transparent to implementations that do not support these options.
sections.eli5: Each letter now begins with a short name tag, either short or long, so the reader knows which project it is for.

sections.title: Choosing an ExID
sections.content:
The designer picks the ExID at design time. It MUST be 16 or 32 bits, stored in big-endian byte order. Designers SHOULD use 16-bit ExIDs to save option space, unless they need 32 bits to avoid false positives or to keep alignment with an expected future assigned codepoint.

IANA registers ExIDs first come, first served on the first two bytes, so all ExIDs MUST be unique based on their first 16 bits. In a 32-bit ExID the second two bytes act as a magic number, a self-selected value chosen mainly because others are unlikely to pick it. It also keeps the option contents at the same byte alignment they would have under a normal assigned codepoint.

The cost is that the ExID uses TCP option space, and the 32-bit form uses more but protects better against false positives.
sections.eli5: Short tags save room on the envelope, and long tags are harder to confuse with someone else's. You pick whichever fits your project, and the first person to claim a tag keeps it.

sections.title: How Receivers Process the Option
sections.content:
During TCP processing, the ExID in an experimental option is matched against the ExIDs of each implemented protocol. Options whose ExID matches no implemented protocol MUST be ignored.

The ExID must be coordinated during connection setup like any option. If an ExID is used in any segment of a connection, it MUST be present in the SYN segments of that connection. It SHOULD be used in all segments of that connection that carry an experimental option.

The RFC accepts the extra header space and processing, because these are experiments and a finished protocol can later get a dedicated codepoint.
sections.eli5: Each reader checks the name tag and throws away letters that are not for any project they run. Everyone has to start using tags from the very first letter of the conversation.

sections.title: False Positives and Migration
sections.content:
A false positive happens when a registered ExID matches the value of an option that does not use ExIDs, so the wrong routine reads it. Experiments that are not robust to this SHOULD add other detection, such as checksums or minimal digital signatures over the options they support.

When an experiment later gets an assigned codepoint, the protocol SHOULD NOT keep using an ExID with it. The RFC recommends no specific migration plan. A segment MUST NOT contain both the assigned option and the experimental option for the same protocol, to conserve option space. A TCP wanting backward compatibility might instead send multiple SYNs with alternate options and keep the most desired successful connection.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a stranger's note might happen to start with your tag by accident, so add a check. Once your project gets its own real mailbox, stop using tags and do not use both at once.

sections.title: The IANA ExID Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "TCP Experimental Option Experiment Identifiers (TCP ExIDs)" registry. It records both 16-bit and 32-bit ExIDs with a reference for each, and ExIDs apply to both option 253 and 254. Entries are first come, first served, judged on the first two bytes of the ExID.

The RFC gives collision examples: 0x12340000 collides with an earlier 0x1234abcd, 0x5678 collides with 0x56780123, and 0xabcd1234 collides with 0xabcd. IANA should require only the desired value and a point of contact, and will record known duplicate uses to help debugging.
sections.eli5: A list keeper writes down who claimed which tag. If your tag starts the same as someone else's, you pick another.

sections.title: Rationale and Security
sections.content:
ExIDs mix an IANA first come, first served registry with magic numbers, since people often fail to register or squat. The RFC considered IEEE OUIs, which are 24-bit identifiers already longer than the short ExID and costly to obtain, and IANA Private Enterprise Numbers, which are free but assigned to organizations and may be larger than needed.

On security, the RFC says the mechanism neither enhances nor weakens existing TCP option security.
sections.eli5: The authors looked at other ID systems but they were too big or too costly, so they built a small tag instead. It does not make things safer or less safe.
